---
title: "Environmental amounts and balances exercises"
---

Use the values given; do not look up other constants. Predict the direction of change before calculating.

## 1. Mixing without loss

Mix 4.00 L at 2.00 mg/L with 1.00 L of solute-free water. Find the inventory and final concentration. What caused the decrease?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Balance mg first, then divide by the final volume.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
The initial and final inventory is **8.00 mg**. Final concentration is **1.60 mg/L**. Dilution lowers concentration without consuming solute.
:::

## 2. A river load

A stream carries 0.200 m³/s at 0.500 mg/L. Calculate its solute load in g/s and kg/day. Use 1000 L/m³ and 86400 s/day.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Convert flow to L/s before multiplying.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
The flow is 200 L/s, giving 100 mg/s = **0.100 g/s**, or **8.64 kg/day**. This assumes the flow and concentration remain constant over the day.
:::

## 3. A two-phase bottle

A sealed bottle initially contains 10.0 mg of parent compound in water. Later, water contains 4.0 mg and sediment contains 5.0 mg. Sampling removes nothing. What amount is unaccounted for? Can you identify its fate?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Sum the measured parent inventories across both phases.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Measured parent totals **9.0 mg**, leaving **1.0 mg** unaccounted for. Transformation, unmeasured bottle-wall retention, and analytical error are candidates. The balance alone does not establish mineralisation or elemental loss.
:::

## 4. Interpret the boundary

A lake concentration falls while its volume rises. What measurements would distinguish dilution, export, and chemical transformation?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Track volumes, flows, phase inventories, and chemical identities.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Worked solution"}
Measure volume and total inventory, inlet/outlet loads, relevant solid-phase amounts, and plausible transformation products over a consistent period. A concentration series alone does not close the balance.
:::

## Explore: a lake approaching steady state {#explore}

Predict what happens to the steady-state inventory if the solute input doubles,
and what happens if the water flow doubles instead. Then change one input at a
time and compare the curve, the time constant and the balance table.

```{=html}
<link rel="stylesheet" href="../demos/demo.css">
<div data-demo="boxmodel" role="group" aria-label="Well-mixed lake approaching steady state">
<p>Reference case: V = 1.0 × 10⁶ m³ and Q = 1.0 × 10⁴ m³/day give V/Q = 100 days. An input of 1.0 kg/day gives a steady inventory of 100 kg (0.10 mg/L); after 100 days the lake holds 63 kg.</p>
</div>
<script src="../demos/core.js"></script>
<script src="../demos/boxmodel.js"></script>
```

**E1.** Choose **Worked example**. Read the balance table at steady state. Which
fluxes are still running, and why does the inventory not change? Then choose
**Double the input** and check the new steady inventory by hand.

**E2.** Reset, then raise the lake volume to 4 million m³ while keeping the flow
and input fixed. What happens to the steady concentration, and what happens to
the time needed to get there? Explain both with V/Q.

**E3.** Choose **Flush with clean water**, then **Flushing plus reaction**. How
much of the 100 kg is left after one time constant in each case? Explain why
seeing only the falling curve cannot tell you how much was flushing and how much
was reaction.

### Model conditions and hand check

The constructed lake has V = 1.0 × 10⁶ m³, Q = 1.0 × 10⁴ m³/day in and out, and
an input of 1.0 kg/day of a conservative solute, starting clean. The replacement
time is `V/Q = 10⁶ / 10⁴ = 100 days`. At steady state output equals input, so
`Q × C = 1.0 kg/day` and `C = 1.0 / 10⁴ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ kg/m³ = 0.10 mg/L`, an
inventory of **100 kg**. Starting from a clean lake, the inventory after one
replacement time is `100 × (1 − e⁻¹) = 63 kg`.

With a first-order reaction the two loss rates add: `Q/V + k`. For k = 0.010 per
day this doubles the total loss rate, halving both the time constant (50 days)
and the steady inventory (50 kg). Flushing 100 kg with clean water leaves
`100 × e⁻¹ = 37 kg` after 100 days by flushing alone, and `100 × e⁻² = 14 kg`
with the reaction added.

The lake is well mixed, so the outlet concentration equals the lake
concentration. Volume, flow and input are constant, the inflow carries no other
solute than the stated input, and the only reaction is first order. Sorption to
sediment, exchange with air and seasonal changes in flow are not included.
